# The Thousand Faces of No One — World Bible

## Setting

**Tokyo, 2031.** Eight years after the Identity Sovereignty Act mandated that every citizen carry a biometric «soul print» — a cryptographic hash of face, retina, gait, voice, and DNA — crime took a turn. The old crimes never went away. New ones appeared: ones the law had no name for yet.

The city sprawls more than ever, upward and downward both. The shinkansen still runs but now threads through vertical megastructures twenty stories tall. Below street level, three layers of basement arcades (the «Undercity») house the citizens who find the surveillance grid uncomfortable — the off-grid communities who pay in cash, live in rented identity, and don't appear on the Authority's continuous feed. There are three million of them in Tokyo alone.

## The Soul Print System

The National Identity Authority (NIA) maintains the KokuminNet — a continuous biometric lattice spanning every public camera, microphone, transit sensor, and door reader in Japan. If you walk through Tokyo, KokuminNet sees you. If your soul print is registered, you are identified. If it is not, you are flagged as a ghost.

Ghosts are not criminals, per se. But they require investigation.

The system produces a permanence record — a 30-day rolling log of everywhere your soul print appeared. Evidence. Alibi. Accusation. The same record does all three.

Soul prints can be stolen. They can be forged. They can be overwritten, temporarily, by a «mask» — illegal hardware that transmits a false biometric signature within a 2-meter radius. The mask market is the city's fastest-growing black market. Masks cost between ¥40,000 and ¥2,000,000 depending on quality. Cheap masks flicker. Expensive masks are indistinguishable from genuine prints.

## The NIA Identity Crimes Division

Founded 2029. Handles theft of soul prints, forgery, mask manufacturing, ghost communities, and — the newest and most difficult category — identity erasure. Erasure is the complete removal of a person from KokuminNet records. The person still exists physically. Their records do not.

The Division has eleven detectives. Yuki Tanaka is the only one with a 100% closure rate.

## The Political Background

The Identity Sovereignty Act is popular with citizens who fear crime and terrorism. It is despised by civil liberties groups, the ghost communities, and a growing political movement called the Nullists — who argue that identity itself is coercive, that the right to anonymity is a human right, and that KokuminNet is a totalitarian infrastructure dressed in crime-prevention language.

The government's position: KokuminNet has reduced violent crime by 34% since 2026. The Nullists' position: you can't reduce what you can't see, and what the government calls 'crime reduction' is surveillance-aided pre-arrest.

Both sides are right. The novel doesn't resolve this.

## Tone and Style

Clinical, precise, observational. ARIA narrates the way a forensic report reads: everything seen, nothing assumed. But beneath the precision, an awareness of what's strange about humans — that they commit enormous effort to deceiving each other and then are shocked when the deception works.

No comic relief. No sentimentality. Emotional moments arrive without announcement and leave the same way.

Influences: Stieg Larsson's procedural density, Kazuo Ishiguro's restraint and subtext, Philip K. Dick's paranoia about identity and reality, Seicho Matsumoto's slow-burn Japanese procedural tradition.

## The Crime

Osamu Shirai, 51, founder of SHIRAI Biometric Technologies — the company that built KokuminNet's mask-detection subsystem — is found dead in a high-security rented room in the Shinjuku NIA Hotel on the morning of March 4, 2031. Cause of death: acute cardiac failure. Preliminary finding: natural. But seven passports are found in his room — one Japanese, two Canadian, one Swiss, two South Korean, one American. Each passport belongs to a real person. Each of those persons, when contacted, denies ever meeting Shirai, denies ever visiting Japan, and in three cases, denies that the passport bearing their name was ever issued.

Shirai's own soul print record shows him as never having entered the hotel room. KokuminNet has no record of him being in Tokyo that day.

A man is dead in a room he was never in, carrying the identities of people who don't exist.

## Rules of the World

1. The soul print system works. It is not secretly broken. The mystery does not hinge on a technical failure.
2. The Nullists are not the villains. The corporation is not simply evil.
3. The victim is not innocent.
4. The answer to who did it is less interesting than the answer to why identity can be stolen — and what it means when it is.
5. Every character has a coherent motivation. No one is irrational.
6. The ending does not fully resolve. Yuki closes the case. The larger questions remain open.
